Constraints and tenant boundaries
Deep dive
About 12 minutes
AI-generated

A constraint makes a rule part of the table’s definition. A positive order-line quantity, an order number used only once and a product reference that reaches an existing product are different rules, but they share one useful property: the database can refuse a write that breaks them. The checkout application, an import and an administrator’s SQL all meet the same boundary.

Choosing that boundary starts with the state you want to forbid. “A line has a positive quantity” concerns one row. “No two lines have the same order and line number” compares identities across rows. “This line belongs to an order in the same shop” follows a reference. Each needs a declaration that expresses the whole rule.

The examples use PostgreSQL 18 and the shop from the introduction. Later, a labelled tenant variant lets the application serve two shops. It reveals why a reference that merely reaches an existing row can still be the wrong reference. The figure illustrates reference matching; the downloadable SQL checks their accepted and rejected cases on PostgreSQL 18.6.

Rules about one row
One identity, one row
A reference in both directions
The shop is part of the identity
Integrity does not grant access
Rules that need a protocol
Trying the boundary
Rules about one row

Order 103’s first line contains one blue mug. Its quantity must be present and greater than zero. Those are two separate requirements:

quantity integer NOT NULL
  CONSTRAINT
    order_items_quantity_positive
  CHECK (quantity > 0)

NOT NULL refuses an absent quantity. CHECK evaluates a condition for the row being inserted or changed. Here it refuses zero and negative quantities. Naming the check gives an error a useful identity: order_items_quantity_positive says which rule failed.

As Values, missing data and equality showed, a PostgreSQL check rejects false and accepts true or unknown. A missing quantity makes quantity > 0 unknown, so the check alone would allow it. The two declarations work together.

Four attempted quantities under that definition
Quantity	Positive check	Result
1	True	Allowed
0	False	Refused
−1	False	Refused
NULL	Unknown	Refused by NOT NULL

A check can use several columns of the same row. The shop’s status check allows only pending, paid and cancelled. A table storing two ends of an interval could require its end to follow its start. Neither rule needs to read another row.

The declaration says exactly that much. Allowing the word paid does not establish that the order has enough payments. Requiring stock >= 0 does not establish that every sale reduced stock. A constraint can preserve a property of the stored representation without proving the whole business process correct.

A default is different again. DEFAULT 'pending' supplies a status when an insert omits it; it does not restrict what an explicit value may be. Keep the check if other statuses must be impossible.

One identity, one row

The rule for line identity concerns a pair. Order 103 has lines 1 and 2, and order 101 also has a line 1. The database must permit those repetitions while refusing another line 1 on order 103:

PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no)

This primary key makes the pair unique and requires both columns. Separate declarations of UNIQUE (order_id) and UNIQUE (line_no) would mean something else: at most one line per order, and at most one line numbered 1 in the entire table. Composite means that the combination is the identity.

UNIQUE can preserve another identity beside the primary key. If a variant introduces a generated line_id, it still needs UNIQUE (order_id, line_no) and required values for that business identity. Generating different IDs for two inserts does not stop them recording the same line twice. Relations, keys and normalisation develops the choice of keys; constraints carry that choice into every write.

The comparison rule matters too. Uniqueness on text uses the column’s equality rules, so a rule that considers two spellings the same must be reflected in the constrained value or its comparison. Ordinary PostgreSQL uniqueness also permits several missing values. Use NOT NULL for a required identity; choose NULLS NOT DISTINCT when an optional unique value should allow at most one absence.

A preflight query is not the key

For a separate insertion experiment, start with line (103, 1) absent. A checkout writer and an import both intend to create it. Each can ask whether the line exists and get no row before either inserts it. A check in application code has now passed twice.

One possible schedule for two writers of the same line identity
Step	Checkout writer	Import writer
1	Finds no (103, 1)	Finds no (103, 1)
2	Inserts (103, 1); transaction remains open	
3		Attempts the same key; waits
4	Commits	Duplicate-key error; rolls back

With an immediate primary key, PostgreSQL’s second insert waits for the conflicting transaction’s outcome. If the first commits and keeps the row, the second is refused. If the first rolls back, the second can proceed. The key’s enforcement includes the overlap that the separate lookup missed.

A disposable PostgreSQL 18.6 run checked the commit case: the second insert waited on the first transaction, then received a duplicate-key error, and one row remained. Without the key, two empty preflight results followed by two inserts left two copies. This is a constraint doing concurrent enforcement, rather than a reason to avoid constraints whenever transactions overlap.

A reference in both directions

An order line’s product_id names a product. A foreign key makes the database preserve that connection:

product_id text NOT NULL
  REFERENCES products (product_id)

The parent, products, must offer a unique identity for the reference to target. Its primary key does that. The child, order_items, can repeat P7 on many lines, because each is a separate purchase of that product. The foreign key requires a match; it does not make the child’s product ID unique.

Enforcement works in both directions. Inserting a line for a nonexistent product is refused. Changing a line to that product is refused too. On the parent side, deleting P7 or changing its key would leave existing lines pointing nowhere, so the database must either refuse the change or carry out a declared action that preserves the rule.

With the core schema’s default action, deleting P7 while its lines remain fails. The same is true of deleting order 103 while its lines remain. The foreign keys protect those relationships; they do not decide whether the shop ought to retain an order forever.

What a delete should mean

An order line is a component of an order. If a separate deletion policy allows an order and all its lines to be removed together, the order reference can say so:

FOREIGN KEY (order_id)
  REFERENCES orders (order_id)
  ON DELETE CASCADE

CASCADE removes the child lines when their order is deleted. Applying that action to the product reference would have a different consequence: deleting a catalogue product would erase lines from old purchases. The references look similar, but the relationships mean different things.

PostgreSQL foreign-key actions when a referenced parent is deleted
Action	Effect on referencing rows
NO ACTION, the default	The reference must be valid when checked; otherwise the delete fails.
RESTRICT	Refuses deleting a referenced parent without postponing that check.
CASCADE	Deletes the referencing rows.
SET NULL or SET DEFAULT	Changes the reference; the resulting row must still satisfy its other rules.

SET NULL suits an optional association, rather than the required product on this line. It cannot override NOT NULL. A default is no escape either: a non-missing default reference still needs its parent. ON UPDATE actions make the corresponding choice when the parent’s referenced key changes.

References also need a practical access path. PostgreSQL creates an index for a primary or unique key, but does not automatically create one on the child’s foreign-key columns. Deleting a product requires finding its lines. On a large line table an index on product_id can make that search cheaper; the line primary key already starts with order_id for the order-side search. Indexes and access paths develops that cost.

When the reference may be checked at commit
The shop is part of the identity

Now enter the collection’s tenant-scoped variant. The application serves shop 10, the original shop, and shop 20, Harbour Tea. Each shop is a tenant: one customer organisation whose data shares the application with others. Mina is a customer of shop 10; she is not a tenant herself.

Shop 10’s P7 is the Blue mug at 20.00. Shop 20 has its own P7, a Copper mug at 18.00. P7 alone no longer identifies a product. The pair (shop_id, product_id) does. Orders are identified by (shop_id, order_id), and lines by (shop_id, order_id, line_no).

A line therefore needs the shop ID in its references as well as its own key. These small definitions show the identity and reference columns; descriptive order columns and the customer reference are omitted here. The worksheet includes the same-shop customer reference and the line’s quantity and price.

CREATE TABLE products (
  shop_id integer,
  product_id text,
  name text NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (shop_id, product_id)
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  shop_id integer,
  order_id integer,
  PRIMARY KEY (shop_id, order_id)
);
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  shop_id integer,
  order_id integer,
  line_no integer,
  product_id text NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (
    shop_id, order_id, line_no
  ),
  FOREIGN KEY (shop_id, order_id)
    REFERENCES orders (
      shop_id, order_id
    ),
  FOREIGN KEY (shop_id, product_id)
    REFERENCES products (
      shop_id, product_id
    )
);

The same shop_id participates in both foreign keys. A line in shop 10 must find both an order in shop 10 and a product in shop 10. Giving the line independent shop IDs for its order and product would let those two parents belong to different shops unless another rule tied the IDs together.

Figure 1 follows the mug line on order 103. Start with shop 10, then change the attempted line’s shop to 20. Watch the two lookups separately: the product exists in both shops, but the order does not.

The relevant parent rows from the tenant variant. Shop 10 follows the stored mug line on order 103. Shop 20 is an invalid attempted line: its product exists, but order (20, 103) does not. The steps illustrate reference matching, not PostgreSQL’s check order or a complete insert.
The two lookups, as text

At shop 10 the line reaches order (10, 103) and the Blue mug (10, P7). At shop 20 it reaches the Copper mug, but there is no order (20, 103). The order foreign key refuses that attempted line. Finding order 103 in shop 10 cannot satisfy a reference asking for shop 20.

This is more than putting a shop label on a row. Every tenant-owned relationship must carry the scope: an order to its customer, a line to its order and product, a payment to its order. In this variant the order-to-customer reference is FOREIGN KEY (shop_id, customer_id) REFERENCES customers (shop_id, customer_id). Keeping an old unscoped reference leaves that relationship outside the boundary.

PostgreSQL will not accept REFERENCES products (product_id) against the composite product key above: product_id alone is not unique. Adding global uniqueness merely to make that declaration work would prohibit the two valid P7s. Preserve the intended identity, then reference all of it.

Queries need the same meaning. A join on i.product_id = p.product_id would pair shop 10’s mug line with both P7 products. Include i.shop_id = p.shop_id in that match. Foreign keys protect stored relationships; they do not insert the missing condition into a query.

Required and optional pairs

The tenant line’s primary key already requires its shop and order IDs, and product_id is explicitly NOT NULL. Those required values matter. Under PostgreSQL’s default MATCH SIMPLE, a composite reference with any missing component does not require a parent match. A nullable product ID could therefore leave a line with no checked product reference at all.

For a wholly optional composite association, MATCH FULL allows either a complete matching pair or an entirely missing pair; it rejects a half-missing pair. It still permits both values to be missing. The shop’s required product association needs required columns, rather than treating a missing pair as another way to pass.

Integrity does not grant access

The composite foreign keys answer whether stored relationships stay inside one shop. They do not answer whether the caller is entitled to act for that shop. A caller allowed to insert arbitrary values could supply a completely consistent shop 20 order and product pair. Every reference could pass while the caller had no authority over Harbour Tea.

The application must establish the caller’s authorised shop and carry that identity through its requests. Database privileges determine which operations its connection may perform. In PostgreSQL, row security policies can additionally restrict which rows that connection may read or change. These are access rules applied under a particular runtime identity, with their own behaviour for owners and privileged roles.

Keeping those questions distinct makes testing clearer. Try a shop 10 line with a parent from another shop to test integrity. Try a well-formed shop 20 operation through a shop 10 caller to test authority. The latter should fail even though the data would be internally consistent. Database access and least privilege develops runtime authority; PostgreSQL roles, policies and privileged code works through policy tests.

Rules that need a protocol

The shop can declare a positive payment amount and a reference to an order. Neither declaration establishes that an order marked paid has enough payments. If marking an order paid must mean that its payments cover its line total, that rule compares several changing rows, and a write affecting any of them could change its truth.

PostgreSQL row checks are not a supported way to enforce such a rule by reading other rows. Hiding that read in a function does not make it safe: changing a different row does not cause the original row’s check to run again. The same problem applies to a time-dependent check that is expected to become false merely because the clock advances.

Look first for a declarative form the engine supports. A unique key already expresses a cross-row rule. A foreign key expresses an existence rule. PostgreSQL exclusion constraints can forbid certain conflicting pairs, such as overlapping reservations for the same room. These declarations have enforcement designed for their particular relationships.

A class-session capacity limit is different: count several booking rows and keep the total within the session’s capacity. Two transactions can both count a free place before either adds its booking. Each new row can pass all its own checks while the combined result exceeds capacity. A trigger that simply repeats that count can make the same mistake.

Such a rule needs a complete write protocol: which changes belong in one transaction, how competing writers coordinate, what each reads after waiting and which failures require a complete retry. The introduction’s conditional stock update is one protocol for one stock row; it is not a general solution to counting bookings. Transactions and isolation develops these concurrent multi-row rules.

Keep the simpler constraints alongside that protocol. A booking protocol should not also have to remember to reject every missing reference or duplicate identity itself. Declarations preserve the parts they can express; transaction logic carries the remaining business rule.

Trying the boundary

Test a constraint with a valid write and the smallest write that would break its promise. For a composite key, repeat the whole key and also repeat just one component in a valid new combination. For a reference, try an absent parent, a changed child reference and a parent deletion. For tenant scope, use a parent that exists in the other shop; an entirely nonexistent ID would not distinguish a scoped reference from an unscoped one.

Check the returned error as well as the unchanged data. PostgreSQL reports 23502 for a not-null violation, 23514 for a check violation, 23505 for uniqueness and 23503 for a foreign key. Drivers expose the SQLSTATE and relevant object fields. Use those fields and named constraints to recognise an expected refusal, rather than parsing the wording of an error message.

In an explicit PostgreSQL transaction, an ordinary statement error leaves the transaction failed until it is rolled back, or recovered to an appropriate savepoint. The application should turn the refusal into a meaningful result and end or recover that transaction. Repeating the same invalid write is not a useful retry strategy.

Download the PostgreSQL worksheet to repeat the row, identity, reference, deletion and tenant examples with psql -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f constraints.sql. It creates temporary objects, checks expected refusals by SQLSTATE and rolls the work back. Counterexamples remove the relevant rule so that the difference is visible. The separate concurrent-key run used two writer connections to a disposable local server; it is described above rather than claimed by this single-session download.

Joins and the meaning of a result row
Deep dive
About 8 minutes
AI-generated

A join returns a row for each matching pair of input rows. That small rule explains both its usefulness and its most expensive mistakes. Adding a customer name to each order may leave the row count unchanged. Adding payments to order lines may multiply it. Both queries can be valid SQL, and both can return plausible amounts.

The first question is therefore what one result row should mean. A receipt wants one row per order line. A list of orders wants one per order. A list of customers who have ordered wants one per customer, however many orders they have. Keep that meaning in view while choosing the matches.

This article builds the shop’s still-due report: the value of each order, its recorded payments and the difference. It uses PostgreSQL 18 and the same three orders as the introduction. The figures illustrate result construction; the downloadable SQL checks the results on PostgreSQL 18.6.

One row for each match
Two independent collections
Total before combining
Keeping unmatched rows
Whether a match exists
Checking the question
One row for each match

Begin with orders and customers. Each order carries a customer_id, and the customer primary key makes that value unique on the other side.

SELECT o.order_id, c.name
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;
One result row per order
Order	Customer
101	Mina Shah
102	Tariq Aziz
103	Mina Shah

Order 101 finds Mina, order 102 finds Tariq, and order 103 finds Mina again. Mina appears twice because she has two orders. These are different order rows carrying the same customer fact, rather than duplicate customers in the source table.

The key tells us that each order finds at most one customer. The non-missing foreign key tells us that the customer exists, so in this schema every order finds exactly one. A join condition alone promises neither. Joining on a non-unique name could find several people, and joining to an optional relation could find none.

Now join orders to their lines instead. Order 101 has two matching lines, 102 has one and 103 has two. The result has five rows. One row now means one order line, identified by (order_id, line_no). The order’s date and customer ID repeat on each of its lines because they describe the order to which those lines belong.

This meaning is often called the result’s grain. Write it as “one row per …” before adding a sum or another join. It gives you a concrete check: if one row should mean an order, why does order 101 appear twice?

Two independent collections

Order 101 has two lines, worth 4.50 and 35.00, and two payments, 30.00 and 9.50. The line numbers identify what was bought. The payment IDs identify payments towards the order; no payment belongs to a particular line.

Joining these collections on order_id therefore matches every line with every payment for that order. Read the four pairs in the drawing, then choose Total each side first.

Every line matches both payments on order_id. Read down either amount: each original contribution appears twice.

The matches as text

The detailed join has four rows: two lines times two payments. With three lines and four payments, it would have twelve. The match is a pair of facts about the same order, not evidence that one payment paid for that particular line.

SELECT i.order_id,
       SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total,
       SUM(p.amount) AS paid
FROM order_items AS i
JOIN payments AS p ON p.order_id = i.order_id
GROUP BY i.order_id
ORDER BY i.order_id;

For 101 this reports 79.00 for the order and 79.00 paid. Subtracting gives zero, the correct balance for the wrong reason. Order 102 also looks correct because it has one line and one payment. Order 103 disappears because it has no payment. Testing only a single-line paid order would miss both defects.

GROUP BY does not undo the multiplication. It adds the values on the rows it receives, including every repeated contribution. Nor does SUM(DISTINCT amount) repair it. That removes repeated values, so two legitimate payments of the same amount would be counted once. The identities are different even when their amounts agree.

SELECT DISTINCT removes identical projected result rows. It is useful when that is the requested answer, but it cannot decide which line or payment each amount belongs to. Keep the right identities through the calculation instead of asking a duplicate-removal step to reconstruct them.

Total before combining

The report wants one row per order, so first make each collection have that grain. Total the lines by order_id, and separately total payments by order_id. Each derived result then has at most one row for any order. Combining them cannot multiply an order’s amounts.

WITH lets us name these intermediate query results. Such a name is a common table expression, or CTE. It is available to this statement, rather than being a stored report table.

WITH line_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS order_total
  FROM order_items
  GROUP BY order_id
), payment_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS paid
  FROM payments
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT o.order_id, c.name, l.order_total,
       COALESCE(p.paid, 0::numeric) AS paid,
       l.order_total - COALESCE(p.paid, 0::numeric) AS due
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
LEFT JOIN line_totals AS l ON l.order_id = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN payment_totals AS p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;
The still-due report, using recorded line prices and payments
Order	Order total	Paid	Due
101	39.50	39.50	0.00
102	40.00	40.00	0.00
103	29.00	0.00	29.00

Order 101 now combines one line-total row with one payment-total row. Order 103 has a line total but no payment-total row. A LEFT JOIN retains its order row and supplies NULL for the missing payment columns. COALESCE turns that missing total into zero: no recorded payments contributed to it.

We do not apply the same substitution to a missing line total. This schema does not enforce that every order has a line. An order with no lines would remain in this report with a missing total and balance, signalling that its value has not been established. Treating it as a free order would be a different business rule. The three core orders all have lines.

The calculation uses the agreed unit_price on each line. Joining today’s product price into the sum would change old receipts when the catalogue changed. Likewise, the status text is not a substitute for summing payments. Here 101 and 102 are paid, but a status field does not prove that recorded amounts equal what is owed.

The CTEs make the reasoning readable. They do not require PostgreSQL to execute the clauses as a series of stored temporary tables. The planner may combine work while preserving the result. Query execution and bad plans follows the physical choices; Aggregates, windows and ordered results develops the grouped calculations.

Keeping unmatched rows

An ordinary JOIN, also called an inner join, retains matches only. A left join additionally keeps each left-side row with no match, filling the right side with missing values. It does not add one missing row alongside existing matches. If an order has two matching payments, it still produces two result rows.

That preservation happens at the join. A later WHERE can discard the preserved row again. Suppose we want every order alongside its card payments, if any. Compare the position of the card condition in the next figure.

FIGURE 2 Where does the card condition act?
In ON
In WHERE

ON p.order_id = o.order_id AND p.method = 'card'

Orders after the left join and filter
Order	Payment	Amount
101	501	30.00
102	503	40.00
103	NULL	NULL

Order 103 has no card match. The left join preserves it, with missing payment columns.

Both answers as text
SELECT o.order_id, p.payment_id, p.amount
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN payments AS p
  ON p.order_id = o.order_id AND p.method = 'card'
ORDER BY o.order_id, p.payment_id;

In ON, the condition defines a match. Order 103 has no card payment, so the left join keeps it with missing payment columns. Move p.method = 'card' to WHERE, and it tests the joined rows instead. The condition on 103 is unknown, and WHERE retains only true, so 103 disappears.

Adding OR p.payment_id IS NULL in WHERE is not generally equivalent to putting the card restriction in ON. An order with only non-card payments already found matches at the join, so no missing placeholder row was created. The later filter would remove every one of those matches and lose the order. Make the join’s matching rule express the optional fact you want.

A condition on the preserved side can still belong in WHERE. For example, WHERE o.customer_id = 1 deliberately selects Mina’s orders while retaining missing payments on them. Decide whether each condition chooses the parent rows, defines an optional match or filters the final result.

A right join preserves the right input instead. A full join preserves unmatched rows from both sides, useful for comparing two independently supplied lists. Neither changes the pairing rule. Choosing a different outer join will not make two many-sided collections safe to sum together.

Whether a match exists

Sometimes we need no columns from the other side. “Which customers have ordered?” asks whether an order exists for each customer. Joining customers to orders would return Mina twice. EXISTS tests for at least one matching row without adding a result row for every match.

SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM orders AS o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

The answer is Mina and Tariq, one row each. The inner query refers to c.customer_id from the outer query; this makes it a correlated subquery. SELECT 1 is conventional because only the existence of a result matters. It does not count orders or choose a particular one.

Reverse the test with NOT EXISTS to find customers without orders: Edda. For orders without any payment, change the outer table and the matching condition:

SELECT o.order_id
FROM orders AS o
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM payments AS p
  WHERE p.order_id = o.order_id
)
ORDER BY o.order_id;

This returns 103. It asks a different question from “which orders still have an amount due?” A partly paid order has a payment, so it fails this absence test while still owing money. To find positive balances, name the completed report as another CTE and filter its due > 0. In the core snapshot both questions happen to select 103.

The matching condition is essential. Without p.order_id = o.order_id, the query asks whether the entire payments table is empty. Since payment 501 exists, every order would fail NOT EXISTS, including 103.

A left join followed by WHERE p.payment_id IS NULL can express the same absence test. Test a right-side column guaranteed non-missing in a real match, such as its primary key. A nullable note or reference could be missing on a real payment and would give a false absence.

NOT IN needs more care. If its right-hand result contains a NULL, an otherwise unmatched value can produce unknown rather than true. The shop’s payments.order_id is non-missing, but a later union or optional relation could change that guarantee. NOT EXISTS keeps “no matching row” explicit; Values, missing data and equality follows the three-valued comparisons.

Checking the question

Check a query with rows that separate its possible meanings: a parent with no children, one with one child and one with several children on both joined sides. The shop deliberately contains all three payment shapes. Compare identities as well as totals; a plausible balance can hide doubled contributions.

At each join, identify the key of each input and how many matches a row can find. Before each sum, say what one input row means and whether the same fact has already repeated. Before each absence test, say exactly which match must not exist. These checks continue to work as queries grow, because they follow the meaning of the rows rather than the length of the SQL.

Aggregates, windows and ordered results
Deep dive
About 9 minutes
AI-generated

An aggregate combines values from several rows: a sum of order lines, a count of orders or an average purchase value. A window calculation can put that same kind of answer beside each original row. The difference is whether the rows should collapse into groups or remain individually visible.

Both depend on the input’s meaning. Adding the right amounts from multiplied join rows still gives the wrong total. Ordering brings another choice: two orders placed at the same instant can share a rank, contribute together to a running calculation, or take separate positions in a sequence. Those are different questions.

We start with the shop’s three orders and their agreed line values. Later, two explicitly added orders let us inspect a time tie without inventing more sales amounts. The SQL uses PostgreSQL 18; a downloadable experiment checks the results on PostgreSQL 18.6.

From lines to orders
What is being counted?
Filter inputs or filter groups
Keep the orders
An order within the window
Ties and frames
Positions or shared ranks
From lines to orders

The input table order_items has one row per order line. SUM(quantity * unit_price) adds the amount of each line. GROUP BY order_id makes a separate group for each order, so no line contributes to another order’s total.

SELECT order_id,
       COUNT(*) AS lines,
       SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS order_total
FROM order_items
GROUP BY order_id
ORDER BY order_id;
One output row per order represented in the lines
Order	Lines	Order total
101	2	39.50
102	1	40.00
103	2	29.00

The five input rows have become three output rows. Within a group, order_id has one value, while line number and product can vary. Returning an arbitrary product beside the order total would imply that the whole order belonged to that product. PostgreSQL normally requires selected values to be grouped, aggregated or known to depend on the grouped key; make the intended meaning explicit.

The ORDER BY is separate from grouping. It requests 101, 102, 103 as the display order. GROUP BY itself promises no sorted output, even if a particular plan happens to return groups in key order.

To use these totals in later examples, give them the name order_values with a CTE. Carry each order’s customer and placement time alongside its total:

WITH order_values AS (
  SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.placed_at,
         SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total
  FROM orders AS o
  JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
  GROUP BY o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.placed_at
)
SELECT * FROM order_values ORDER BY order_id;

Every core order has lines, so all three appear. This definition deliberately contains orders whose value can be calculated from their lines; an order without lines would be absent. Decide how to expose incomplete orders in a production report. The earlier join article keeps them visible with a missing total instead of silently calling them zero.

What is being counted?

COUNT(*) counts input rows. COUNT(expression) counts only rows on which that expression is non-missing. The distinction matters after a left join, where an unmatched parent still contributes one row.

SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
       COUNT(*) AS joined_rows,
       COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

Mina has two joined rows and two orders; Tariq has one of each. Edda has one joined row, the placeholder retained by the left join, but zero orders. Counting the non-missing order key answers the question. Counting a nullable order attribute would instead count orders on which that attribute had a value.

SUM and AVG also ignore missing inputs. An aggregate over no input values returns NULL for these functions, while COUNT returns zero. With payments, substituting zero for an empty sum is useful because no recorded payment contributed. With an unknown measurement, substituting zero changes the answer.

The denominator matters for an average. The five line amounts total 108.50, so their mean is 21.70 per line. The same amount spread over three orders gives about 36.17 per order. Neither is a more accurate version of the other. To find mean order value, average the three rows of order_values, rather than the five lines or repeated customer totals.

Filter inputs or filter groups

WHERE chooses rows before aggregation. HAVING chooses completed groups. Suppose we want customers whose orders in the core snapshot are worth at least 50 in total. Group the order values by customer, then test the sum with HAVING.

WITH order_values AS (
  SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id,
         SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total
  FROM orders AS o
  JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
  GROUP BY o.order_id, o.customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id, SUM(order_total) AS customer_total
FROM order_values
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(order_total) >= 50
ORDER BY customer_id;

Mina qualifies with 68.50 from orders 101 and 103. Neither order reaches 50 by itself. WHERE order_total >= 50 would remove both before they could be combined and answer a different question.

A condition that applies to one measure can go inside the aggregate with FILTER. On the orders table, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending') counts pending orders while COUNT(*) still counts every order. Filtering the entire query to pending orders would change both measures. For a day-based report, also choose the time zone and boundaries before filtering; Values, missing data and equality shows why a calendar day is more than a timestamp cast.

Keep the orders

A customer summary has one row per customer. A screen comparing each order with its customer’s total still needs one row per order. Put OVER after an aggregate to make it a window calculation; PARTITION BY customer_id says which other orders belong with the current one.

Switch between the grouped and window results. Watch what happens to order IDs 101 and 103.

FIGURE 1 A total beside a group, or beside each order
GROUP BY customer
Window by customer

Input: orders 101 (Mina, 39.50), 102 (Tariq, 40.00), 103 (Mina, 29.00).

One row per customer with orders
Customer	Total
Mina Shah	68.50
Tariq Aziz	40.00

Mina’s two orders collapse to one group, worth 68.50. The three input rows become two output rows.

Both results as text
WITH order_values AS (
  SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id,
         SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total
  FROM orders AS o
  JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
  GROUP BY o.order_id, o.customer_id
)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_total,
       SUM(order_total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)
         AS customer_total
FROM order_values
ORDER BY order_id;

The window has not changed the grain. Order 101 still means order 101, but can see order 103 when calculating Mina’s total. The same 68.50 appears on both rows. Summing the customer_total output would count Mina’s total twice, so a later consumer must retain that meaning too.

A partition is the set of rows sharing the window’s partition values. It is unrelated to physically partitioning a database table. With no PARTITION BY, all input rows form one partition. With no order inside OVER, this sum covers the whole customer partition at every row.

Windows see the rows that remain after this query level’s WHERE, grouping and HAVING. If we filter order_values to order 103 before applying the window, Mina’s total becomes 29.00. To calculate over all her orders and then display one, put the window calculation in a CTE or subquery and filter its output outside.

An order within the window

Some windows need a sequence. LAG reads a value from the preceding row, and ROW_NUMBER assigns successive positions. Give them an order that says what “preceding” means.

SELECT order_id, customer_id, placed_at,
       LAG(placed_at) OVER (
         PARTITION BY customer_id
         ORDER BY placed_at, order_id
       ) AS previous_order_at
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id, placed_at, order_id;

For Mina’s order 103, the previous instant is 101’s 2026-10-12 09:30Z. For her first order, there is no preceding row, so the result is missing. Tariq’s only order has the same absence. Partitioning prevents his order from becoming Mina’s previous one just because it falls between hers in global time.

The order inside OVER chooses the calculation’s sequence. The final ORDER BY chooses how the result is presented. Write both when both matter; a window’s sort does not promise the output order. Include a unique tie-breaker when individual positions must be stable.

Ties and frames

Now extend the illustration with later orders 105 for Mina and 106 for Edda, both placed at 2026-10-21 12:00:00Z. They have no assigned lines or amounts here and do not alter the earlier still-due report. We need only their identities and times.

Ordering by placed_at alone leaves these two rows tied. They are peers: equal under the window’s ordering expressions. An ordered window aggregate has a default frame, the subset of its partition used for the current calculation. That default runs from the partition’s start through the current row’s last peer.

Choose order 105 in the figure. Compare the default frame with ROWS, with tie-breaker, then move the current row to 106.

FIGURE 2 Which rows does this count include?
Frame

ROWS, with tie-breaker
Whole partition
Current order

count(*) OVER (ORDER BY placed_at)

The five-order illustration, shown in time and ID order
Order	Placed (UTC)	Frame
101	10-12 09:30	included
102	10-14 16:05	included
103	10-20 10:15	included
105 ← current	10-21 12:00	included
106	10-21 12:00	included

Count at this row: 5

Orders 105 and 106 have the same placed_at. The default ordered frame reaches through both peers, so the count at 105 includes both.

Frame membership as text
SELECT order_id, placed_at,
       COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY placed_at) AS through_peers,
       COUNT(*) OVER (
         ORDER BY placed_at, order_id
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS through_row
FROM orders
ORDER BY placed_at, order_id;

The default count is 1, 2, 3, 5, 5. It jumps across both orders at noon together. The explicit ROWS count is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. UNBOUNDED PRECEDING means the start of the partition; CURRENT ROW ends at this row. The tie-breaker makes the fourth row unambiguously 105.

There are two changes in that second expression, and each has a job. ROWS uses row positions rather than peer boundaries. Adding order_id fixes the order of those positions. ROWS alone with ORDER BY placed_at would still allow either tied order to receive count 4. Conversely, adding a unique tie-breaker to the default frame separates these peers and also produces successive counts. Write the frame that expresses the question.

Frames can also look a fixed number of rows back. ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW covers up to three orders, not three days. A time-based frame such as RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, ordered by a single timestamp, covers a time interval and includes ties at its boundaries. An average over orders in that frame still weights orders, not days without orders.

LAST_VALUE is a common surprise. It returns the last value in the current frame, so the default ordered frame usually does not reach the partition’s last row. For the last order ID across the whole sequence, use LAST_VALUE(order_id) OVER (ORDER BY placed_at, order_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING). For a whole-partition sum that needs no sequence, omit the window order altogether.

Positions or shared ranks

ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK answer different tie questions. On the five-order time sequence, the position numbers with the ID tie-breaker are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Ranking on time alone gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 4: the noon orders share fourth place. Dense ranking gives the same numbers in this example, because the tie is last.

The difference appears after a tie. In a separate four-value illustration, scores 40, 30, 30 and 20 have ranks 1, 2, 2, 4 but dense ranks 1, 2, 2, 3. RANK leaves the gap occupied by the tied rows; DENSE_RANK counts distinct peer groups. Do not add an ID to the ranking order when equal scores are supposed to share a rank: the ID would make them different peers. You can still add it to the final display order.

For exactly one latest order per customer, use a position with a deliberate tie-breaker, then filter outside the window calculation:

WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT order_id, customer_id, placed_at,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY customer_id
           ORDER BY placed_at DESC, order_id DESC
         ) AS position
  FROM orders
)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, placed_at
FROM numbered
WHERE position = 1
ORDER BY customer_id;

On the five-order illustration this returns Mina’s 105, Tariq’s 102 and Edda’s 106. If the question instead wants every order tied for a customer’s latest instant, use RANK ordered only by placed_at DESC and keep rank 1. The placement of the tie-breaker follows the business meaning, not a universal rule to append IDs everywhere.

The same care applies when returning only the first few rows. A total order makes their selection deterministic within one view of the data; it does not freeze that view while another transaction changes it. Pagination and consistent exports follows the order across requests.

Pagination and consistent exports
Deep dive
About 9 minutes
AI-generated

A large result usually arrives in pieces. An order list asks for the next page when someone scrolls. An export reads batches until it has written every matching row. Both need an order in which to continue, but they need not make the same promise about changes during the read.

A live list can follow rows after a saved position in the current data. An export may need every value from one consistent view, even while writers continue. A cursor that remembers a position solves the first problem. A snapshot that fixes which versions are visible solves the second.

The examples use PostgreSQL 18 and the shop’s order headers. Extend the three core orders with later orders 105 for Mina and 106 for Edda, both placed at 2026-10-21 12:00:00Z. Both later headers begin with status pending. No lines, payments or stock effects are assigned to those two orders here. The changing-list histories below are separate illustrations and do not amend the core still-due report.

A position in a result

LIMIT caps how many rows a query returns. OFFSET skips that many result rows first. For a page size of two, the first request uses offset zero and the second offset two.

SELECT order_id, placed_at
FROM orders
WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
ORDER BY placed_at, order_id
LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2;

With the five unchanged orders, page one is 101 and 102; page two is 103 and 105. The final order_id breaks the time tie between 105 and 106. Without it, the database can put either noon order first, even without a concurrent change. A total order gives every row a distinct position in this result.

The offset counts positions in the result of this particular query. It has no memory of the previous response. In the next figure, page one has already returned 101 and 102. Cancel 101 between requests, then compare OFFSET 2 with After the saved key.

FIGURE 1 The second page after the list changes

All outcomes as text

After 101 leaves the eligible list, its first two rows are 102 and 103. Skipping two now skips 103 before it has ever been delivered. In a different history, moving 103 before 102 shifts 102 into the second page, so the client receives 102 twice and misses 103. The SQL is correctly applying an offset to a changed result.

Offset pagination can still be a sensible contract for a small, stable result or a screen that accepts movement between numbered pages. It also allows a direct request for page 40 without having visited page 39. Say what stability the application offers; an ordered query alone does not preserve the rows between requests.

Continue after a key

Keyset pagination saves the last row’s ordering values and asks for rows after them. It is also called seek pagination. The cursor is the saved boundary, rather than the number of rows that used to precede it.

Use the pair (placed_at, order_id), the same pair as the ORDER BY. Suppose a larger first page ends at order 105. Its boundary is noon on 21 October and ID 105. This request continues after it:

SELECT order_id, placed_at
FROM orders
WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
  AND (placed_at, order_id) >
      (timestamptz '2026-10-21 12:00:00Z', 105)
ORDER BY placed_at, order_id
LIMIT 2;

The answer is 106. PostgreSQL compares the pair from left to right. A later time qualifies; at the same time, a larger order ID qualifies. In expanded form, the condition is placed_at > saved_time OR (placed_at = saved_time AND order_id > saved_id).

Saving only the timestamp would lose 106: its time is equal, not greater. Changing the test to >= would instead repeat 105 and could keep returning the same first row of a large tie. The unique pair makes strict continuation possible.

Build the cursor from the last row actually returned. On the first request, omit the boundary condition. To indicate that another page exists, an application can request one extra row, return only the page’s requested size and use the last returned row for its cursor. Saving the look-ahead row would skip that row on the next request.

For ORDER BY placed_at DESC, order_id DESC, continuing towards older rows uses < on the pair. Mixed directions need the equivalent explicit branches, with each comparison following its own direction. For a previous page, reverse the comparisons and fetch direction, then reverse the fetched rows for display. Test ties at both boundaries.

The simple pair assumes non-missing keys, as the shop schema supplies. With a nullable sort field, NULLS LAST places missing values but does not make a tuple comparison with NULL true. Define separate continuation branches for the missing-value region, or choose a non-missing order. Text ordering must use the same collation on every request.

What the cursor carries

An API cursor usually packages the boundary into an opaque token. Its contents need to preserve the exact values and the query they belong to: ordering, direction, filters and any shop scope. A timestamp rounded from database microseconds to a coarser application format may move the boundary. Serialise enough precision to compare the same instant again.

Pass decoded values as query parameters, just as for other application inputs. Validate the cursor’s format and version, cap the page size, and reject a cursor supplied for a different filter or order. A signature can detect altered tokens. It does not grant permission to read another shop: apply authorisation and shop restrictions to every query independently.

The token need not point to a row that still exists. Its saved values still define a boundary after that row is cancelled or deleted. This is why cancelling 101 in Figure 1 does not disturb continuation after 102.

A numeric ID alone is a valid boundary only for a list ordered by that ID. An increasing sequence is not proof of commit order: one transaction can allocate a lower number and commit after another. Likewise, a placed_at supplied by an application need not reflect when the database made the row visible.

The work behind a page

An offset also costs work. The server still has to produce the skipped rows. With OFFSET 10000 LIMIT 2, even an index supplying the right order must pass over 10,000 rows before returning the next two. A matching keyset condition can begin at the boundary instead.

On a separate scratch table of 20,000 numbered rows, the experiment’s PostgreSQL index-only scan produced 10,002 rows for that offset query. The equivalent WHERE n > 10000 LIMIT 2 scan produced two. Those are observed row counts on a deliberately simple indexed fixture, not timings or a guarantee that every keyset query reads exactly one page.

The shop list can use an index on (placed_at, order_id). A list restricted to one customer may instead benefit from (customer_id, placed_at, order_id), putting the fixed equality first. Other filters can force the scan to inspect and reject many entries before it finds a full page. Joins, sorting, row visibility and the cost of returned columns still matter. Indexes and access paths develops that match, and Query execution and bad plans checks the work with EXPLAIN.

Keysets trade arbitrary page numbers for efficient continuation. Finding page 40’s boundary still requires a previous boundary, an additional index of saved boundaries or another way to locate it. An exact total count is a separate query over the matching set; the next-page token does not provide it for free.

A boundary is not a snapshot

Return to 103 moves before 102 in Figure 1. Keyset continuation does not repeat 102, but it also cannot find 103 once that row has moved behind the saved boundary. A delivered row moved forwards can appear again. If membership changes, an as-yet unread order can cease to qualify altogether.

Immutable ordering values remove movement of the key, but not all changes to the set. A newly committed row can carry a key behind the boundary. A row can change status before the reader reaches it. Values on already-delivered rows can be changed after they were read. Each request can be internally consistent while the concatenated responses describe no single database view.

For a live browsing list, that may be exactly the intended contract: continue through what currently qualifies, with refresh available to see earlier changes. Deduplicating IDs in the client can suppress repeats but cannot recover omissions. Do not describe this as an exact export of the starting set.

A saved upper time or maximum ID limits how far a traversal goes; it does not freeze it. Late commits can appear below that upper bound, existing rows can change and deletions can remove them. An upper bound works as a complete export boundary only with additional guarantees about how the data is admitted and retained.

One view for an export

An export that promises one consistent view needs to keep that view across batches. PostgreSQL’s ordinary Read Committed queries take a new statement snapshot each time. A read-only Repeatable Read transaction keeps the snapshot established by its first query for later reads.

The next schedule starts afresh with all five eligible orders. The first batch reads 101 and 102. Then a writer cancels 103. Follow the next read under each snapshot choice.

FIGURE 2 Which view supplies the next batch?

The fixed view still includes 103, because it qualified before the writer’s commit. The writer is free to commit; the report’s view remains older. This is the snapshot promise developed in Transactions and isolation, applied to an entire result rather than a repeated stock read.

Keep the export transaction on one database connection. It can issue successive keyset queries, or declare a database cursor and fetch from that one query in batches:

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY;

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled';

DECLARE export_orders NO SCROLL CURSOR FOR
  SELECT order_id, customer_id, placed_at, status
  FROM orders
  WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
  ORDER BY placed_at, order_id;

FETCH FORWARD 2 FROM export_orders;
-- Repeat FETCH until it returns no rows.
CLOSE export_orders;
COMMIT;

This database cursor is a server-side query position, distinct from an API token carrying key values. Its batches continue the same query. A plain non-locking PostgreSQL cursor already keeps its query’s view across fetches; Repeatable Read here also makes the separate count and any related report queries share that view. Starting independent Read Committed queries would not.

The cursor closes at the end of this transaction. A lost connection ends the transaction and its cursor; reopening a new transaction with the last key gets a new snapshot. It can resume a live traversal, but cannot honestly continue the same exact export without another mechanism retaining the original result.

What a long view costs

Old versions visible to an open snapshot cannot yet be removed by PostgreSQL’s normal cleanup. A slow export can therefore retain dead row versions while writers continue, increasing storage pressure and the work cleanup must do later. A cursor limits the rows delivered to the client at once; it does not automatically bound the database’s sorting, retained versions or total work.

Do not leave this transaction open while a person decides whether to click “next”. For a bounded export, read promptly into an output file or other controlled destination, close the transaction, then let the user download that finished result. Limit duration, batch size and concurrency, and handle cancellation by closing the cursor and ending the transaction. Connections, overload and capacity follows the resource budgets.

A durable export job can materialise the required rows from one snapshot, then serve or retry delivery from that stored result. Freeze the actual fields promised by the export. Saving only IDs and later joining them to current orders preserves a membership list, but lets field values change underneath it. Record the export’s query, schema/version and snapshot description alongside the output so its meaning remains clear.

PostgreSQL also offers WITH HOLD cursors that survive a successful commit within the same session. It copies their result into memory or temporary storage. That exchanges snapshot retention for materialisation cost; it is still lost with the session, so it is not a durable background-job record.

Choose the contract before choosing the batching mechanism. A scrolling list usually needs a clear continuation order and honest behaviour under movement. An exact report needs a fixed view, a bounded way to read it and a durable finished output if delivery must survive a retry. Neither “cursor” nor “page size” by itself states all three.

Repeat the experiments

Download the pagination experiment. It uses Python 3’s standard library and an installed PostgreSQL binary directory: python3 run-pagination.py --bindir /path/to/postgresql/bin. The directory needs initdb, pg_ctl, postgres and psql. The script creates and verifies its own temporary cluster on a private local socket, runs the checks, then stops and removes it. It never connects to an existing database.

The experiment contains only the five order headers needed here. Each change resets that input, so cancelling 101, moving 103’s time and cancelling 103 are separate histories. It checks the missing tied row with a timestamp-only boundary, both continuation methods, new and fixed snapshots, cursor fetches and the separate 20,000-row plan comparison. PostgreSQL 18.6 produced the stated outcomes. No throughput, network or distributed-snapshot result is claimed.

SQL at the application boundary
Deep dive
About 10 minutes
AI-generated

A query has a meaning in SQL and a life in the application that sends it. The application supplies values, borrows a connection, reads the answer and decides what to tell its caller. A purchase can use sound SQL and still go wrong if a helper writes on another connection, an empty result is mistaken for success or a timeout leaves work running after the request has gone.

The boundary is a database driver, a library that carries commands and results between application code and a database session. Here the application uses Python with Psycopg 3 and PostgreSQL 18. The syntax belongs to that driver; the questions recur in others. Which parts of the command are values? Who owns the transaction? When has the connection finished its work?

We follow the shop’s orders and products. P7 is the blue mug at 20.00. The examples begin with order 103 already recorded; a later purchase fragment explicitly rewinds to before it. The downloadable experiment checks the driver behaviour on a disposable server. The drawing illustrates the application’s ownership, rather than running a database in the browser.

Send values as values
A result is a contract
One connection owns the transaction
A refused purchase is not a SQL error
A timeout must end the work
The work behind a convenient method
Repeat the driver checks
Send values as values

Suppose a product page receives the product ID P7. SQL needs a condition comparing the product’s key with that value. Building the command by joining strings gives incoming text the same power as SQL you wrote yourself:

# Do not build queries this way.
query = "SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE product_id = '" + product_id + "'"
row = conn.execute(query).fetchone()

For P7, the resulting text happens to be a valid lookup. For P7' OR true --, the inserted quote ends the string value, OR true makes the condition true for every row and -- comments out the closing quote. The caller has changed the question. This is SQL injection.

Give the driver the SQL and its values separately instead:

row = conn.execute(
    "SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE product_id = %s",
    (product_id,),
).fetchone()

%s is Psycopg’s value placeholder. The tuple in the second argument supplies one value; its trailing comma makes it a one-element tuple. Do not put quotes around the placeholder or replace it with Python string formatting. The driver sends a parameter whose value is the supplied text, including any quote marks.

FIGURE 1 The same command, two different values
SQL structure
WHERE product_id = parameter 1
Parameter 1
P7
Matches the Blue mug
Parameter 1
P7' OR true --
Matches no product

The bound text occupies one value position in both cases. Its quote and comment marks do not become SQL operators.

In the native experiment, the concatenated command returned all three products for that incoming text; the parameterised command returned none. It asked for a product with that entire ID, which the shop does not have. A string that merely breaks the unsafe command is also a failure, but this example makes the changed meaning visible without changing any stored data.

Binding preserves the command’s structure. It does not prove that an ID belongs to the caller, that a quantity is sensible or that the query is cheap. Establish the caller’s authority and validate the business input too. In a tenant variant, a safely bound but unauthorised shop ID is still the wrong shop.

Choosing SQL structure

A value placeholder cannot stand for a column name or the keyword DESC. ORDER BY %s with the value price supplies a text value, not a request to sort by the price column. When a screen lets the caller choose a sort, first map the screen’s options to the few structures the application supports.

from psycopg import sql

sort_columns = {"name": "name", "price": "price"}
column = sort_columns[requested_sort]  # reject an unknown option
query = sql.SQL(
    "SELECT product_id, name, price FROM products "
    "ORDER BY {}, product_id LIMIT %s"
).format(sql.Identifier(column))
rows = conn.execute(query, (20,)).fetchall()

Identifier quotes a SQL name correctly. The mapping makes the product decision: these are the two sorts the screen permits. The limit remains a value. If direction is selectable too, choose between fixed ASC and DESC fragments through another mapping. Putting unchecked incoming text into sql.SQL(...) would reopen the original problem.

A result is a contract

The driver converts database values to application values. In this Psycopg configuration, PostgreSQL numeric becomes Python Decimal, an integer becomes int, and SQL NULL becomes None. A returned row is a tuple by default. fetchone() returning None means there is no next row; a row containing a missing column is a tuple containing None. Those are different results.

Decide what the query promises before unpacking it. A lookup by a primary key can return zero or one row. An order-line query can return several. A count returns one row even when the count is zero. Give a missing order, an empty list of orders and a database error distinct meanings in the application.

row = conn.execute(
    "SELECT order_id, status FROM orders "
    "WHERE order_id = %s AND customer_id = %s",
    (order_id, authorised_customer_id),
).fetchone()
if row is None:
    return None  # the caller has no visible matching order
order_id, status = row

The customer ID comes from the application’s established authority, rather than trusting a customer ID beside the order ID in incoming data. Whether an API reveals the difference between an absent order and one the caller may not see is a separate interface choice.

Choose returned columns deliberately. SELECT * lets a schema addition silently change the result’s shape and may fetch large fields the screen never uses. Preserve exact amounts when serialising them to JSON: turning Decimal('20.00') into a binary floating-point number discards the representation chosen for money. A documented decimal string or an explicit fixed-scale representation makes that boundary visible. Timestamp values need an equally deliberate timezone and output format.

fetchall() is convenient for the small lists here. It is also a promise to bring the whole remaining result into application memory. Exports need bounded reading and a defined view of changing data; Pagination and consistent exports develops that contract.

One connection owns the transaction

A connection represents a database session. A transaction belongs to that session, not to the application’s call stack. Two cursors on the same connection share its transaction; two connections do not. A helper that borrows a fresh connection is outside its caller’s transaction even if the helper is called between the caller’s begin and commit.

A pool keeps connections ready to lend to requests. Treat a borrowed connection as a resource owned by one operation until that operation finishes. Pass it into the helpers that participate in the transaction. Do not have those helpers borrow their own connections, commit independently or keep using the borrowed connection after it has been returned.

Psycopg normally starts a transaction even for a plain SELECT. An application that reads, then waits for the next HTTP request can therefore sit idle inside a transaction. This example makes the choice explicit: the pool creates autocommit connections, and each multi-statement operation uses a transaction context.

from psycopg_pool import ConnectionPool

# Create once at application startup; conninfo is deployment configuration.
pool = ConnectionPool(conninfo, kwargs={"autocommit": True}, open=False)
pool.open()
pool.wait(timeout=5)

# During one request:
with pool.connection(timeout=2) as conn:
    with conn.transaction():
        reserve_and_record(conn, purchase)
# Report success only after the transaction context has exited.

# At application shutdown, after requests have finished:
# pool.close()

The outer context borrows and returns the connection. The inner context begins a transaction, commits on a normal exit and rolls back when an exception leaves it. reserve_and_record stands for the complete purchase operation: every reservation, the order and its lines. It receives conn. The pool’s waiting limit bounds acquisition; it is not a limit on the SQL once a connection has been obtained.

Autocommit outside the inner block does not split the statements inside it. Conversely, omitting that block would let each successful write commit separately. Drivers and transaction frameworks have different defaults, so read the actual context-manager contract. In Psycopg, opening conn.transaction() after an implicit transaction has already begun can create a savepoint inside that transaction, rather than owning the outer commit.

Read the paths as text

There is one borrower throughout the active transaction. In the experiment, a helper writing through a second autocommit connection changed the teapot’s price to 36.00 even though the first connection’s stock change rolled back. This separate counterexample changes disposable scratch state; it is not a later event in the shop’s shared history. A rollback can discard only the work in its own transaction.

A refused purchase is not a SQL error

Rewind to before order 103 for the purchase fragment. The mug has stock 1. The conditional update from Transactions and isolation can return one row, or none. Both are successful SQL execution. Only the first means that this attempt reserved stock.

class OutOfStock(Exception):
    pass

def reserve(conn, product_id, quantity):
    if quantity <= 0:
        raise ValueError("quantity must be positive")
    row = conn.execute(
        "UPDATE products SET stock = stock - %s "
        "WHERE product_id = %s AND stock >= %s RETURNING stock",
        (quantity, product_id, quantity),
    ).fetchone()
    if row is None:
        raise OutOfStock(product_id)
    return row[0]

The caller invokes it inside the transaction context for each product, then writes the order and its lines. Catch OutOfStock outside that context so it has already rolled back. Catching it inside and continuing normally would tell the context to commit any earlier successful work. In the experiment, raising an application refusal after reducing P3 restored stock 10 before the same pooled session was borrowed again.

A database error is another path. PostgreSQL reports a stable five-character SQLSTATE; Psycopg exposes it as error.sqlstate, with fields such as error.diag.constraint_name. Use the code and named constraint to recognise an expected refusal. Parsing the English error message depends on wording that may change or be translated.

A check violation such as 23514 usually requires fixing the input or the operation. A serialization failure, 40001, requires rerunning the complete transaction and its decisions. A transport failure during commit can leave the outcome uncertain. These are different instructions, not one generic “retry database error” branch. Retries when a commit reply is missing handles that last distinction.

A timeout must end the work

There are several waits in one request: for a pooled connection, for a lock, for a query result and for commit. An HTTP deadline expiring only says the caller stopped waiting. It does not, by itself, cancel the database command or roll back its transaction.

PostgreSQL’s statement_timeout stops a statement that exceeds its allowed server time, including time spent waiting for a lock. Set it locally inside the transaction when the limit belongs to this operation:

with pool.connection(timeout=2) as conn:
    with conn.transaction():
        conn.execute(
            "SELECT set_config('statement_timeout', %s, true)",
            ("2s",),
        )
        reserve_and_record(conn, purchase)

The third argument to set_config makes the setting local to the transaction, so it expires at its end. Two seconds applies per statement, not to the whole purchase. Choose it within a request budget that also allows acquisition, other statements and cleanup.

In the experiment, a 30 ms statement limit cancelled a deliberate pg_sleep with 57014. Trying an ordinary query before rollback then failed with 25P02, “failed transaction”. Handling the cancellation exception was not enough; the transaction still needed to end. Letting it leave the transaction context performed that rollback.

A caller’s explicit cancellation needs the same ownership discipline. Psycopg’s cancel_safe() requests cancellation through the driver. The experiment waited until its own session was sleeping, cancelled it from another thread, then waited for the query thread and transaction cleanup to finish. Only then did the same connection successfully answer SELECT 1. A cancel request can race with a command finishing, so the command’s eventual result still matters.

Do not return a connection while another task is still using it, or issue a late cancellation against a connection already lent to the next request. If the connection is broken, discard it; the pool can establish a replacement. Replacement restores capacity, not knowledge of an uncertain commit. That purchase still needs resolution before a blind replay.

The work behind a convenient method

An object-relational mapper, or ORM, turns database rows into application objects and generates SQL for operations on them. It can handle parameter binding and connection scopes well. It can also hide the number of commands and the moment a transaction begins.

Consider a page listing 20 orders. A first query gets the orders; accessing each order’s lazily loaded lines then sends one query per order. That is 21 queries for one page, commonly called N+1. It is visible as a repeated remote call even when the application code is a short loop. A batched query for all the selected order IDs can return the lines together.

Fetching everything in one join changes a different thing: the result has one row per line, so order columns repeat. Preserve the row meaning when reconstructing objects and paginating the orders. A query count alone does not establish that the new result is correct. Inspect the generated SQL, its parameters and its transaction boundary, then measure the work for a representative request. Joins and the meaning of a result row supplies the needed result reasoning.

Repeat the driver checks

Download the driver experiment and its shop data into one directory. In a disposable Python environment install psycopg[binary]==3.2.12 and psycopg_pool==3.3.3, then run python run-boundary.py --bindir /path/to/postgresql/bin. The script creates and checks an owned temporary PostgreSQL cluster through a private local socket and removes it afterwards.

Checked with PostgreSQL 18.6, Python 3.14.5, Psycopg 3.2.12 and psycopg_pool 3.3.3. The checks cover bound text, identifier composition, decimal conversion, zero returned rows, implicit transactions, rollback on an application refusal and a constraint error, statement timeout, explicit cancellation and replacement of a closed pooled connection. They are local functional checks, not measurements of production latency, pool sizing or behaviour through a connection proxy.

Transactions and isolation
Deep dive
About 11 minutes
AI-generated

A transaction makes a group of changes all or nothing. Isolation governs how that group interacts with other transactions. The distinction matters whenever a decision depends on a value that another writer can change. Two purchases can each be complete and still sell the same last mug.

The introduction fixed that race with a conditional stock update. Here we use it to separate three promises: keeping the purchase together, deciding which committed data a query sees, and making concurrent decisions agree with some order of taking turns. A stable view of the data supplies the second promise. It does not, by itself, supply the third.

The examples use PostgreSQL 18. They begin with the shop’s purchase, then add two instructors covering a tea class. The drawings follow chosen schedules rather than elapsed time or physical storage. A downloadable experiment repeats the relevant schedules on an owned, disposable PostgreSQL instance.
